Twitter Sentiment Classifier

PSTAT 131

Aaron Chen-Xiao, Yumeng Guo, Sophia Leng, Sahand Shafieha, Olivia Shao

06/12/2026

Data Cleaning

Here is what was done in the data cleaning process:

  1. Added column names per project_memo submitted previously
  2. Checked for the following:
    1. Missing values
    2. Duplicated rows
  3. Checked the levels of columns and removed the columns that had one level and weren’t useful
  4. Split the date column into date and time_pdt
  5. Binarized sentiment
  6. Cleaned up text column
  7. Tokenized and removed stop words for both unigrams and bigrams for future feature extraction
# load the dataset
twitter <- read_csv("sample_50k.csv")
# adding back the column names
colnames(twitter) <- c("sentiment", "id", "date", "query", "user", "text")

# Balanced Dataset
twitter %>%
  count(sentiment)
## # A tibble: 2 × 2
##   sentiment     n
##       <dbl> <int>
## 1         0 25000
## 2         1 25000
# Check for missing values
colSums(is.na(twitter))
## sentiment        id      date     query      user      text 
##         0         0         0         0         0         0
# Check summary stats for sentiment
summary(twitter$sentiment)
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##     0.0     0.0     0.5     0.5     1.0     1.0
# Check for duplicated rows
sum(duplicated(twitter))
## [1] 0
# View levels of query
unique(twitter$query) 
## [1] "NO_QUERY"
# We only have 1 level "NO_QUERY" so we can drop it
twitter_cleaned <- twitter %>% select(-query)

# Split date column into date, time, and time_zone
twitter_cleaned <- twitter_cleaned %>%
  mutate(date_raw = date) %>%
  mutate(
    # Extract timezone before parsing
    time_zone = sub(".*\\s(\\S+)\\s\\d{4}$", "\\1", date_raw),
    
    # Strip timezone from string, then parse
    parsed_dt = parse_date_time(
      sub("(.*?)\\s+\\S+(\\s+\\d{4})$", "\\1\\2", date_raw),
      orders = "a b d H:M:S Y"
    ),
    
    # Extract and format date as MM/DD/YYYY, stored as Date type
    date = as.Date(format(parsed_dt, "%m/%d/%Y"), format = "%m/%d/%Y"),
    
    # Extract time and store as hms
    time = as_hms(format(parsed_dt, "%H:%M:%S"))
  ) %>%
  select(-parsed_dt, -date_raw)

unique(twitter_cleaned$time_zone)
## [1] "PDT"
# I noticed that every time zone in the dataset is in PDT so I drop the column.
# And renamed the time column into time_pdt
twitter_cleaned <- twitter_cleaned %>% select(-time_zone)
twitter_cleaned <- twitter_cleaned %>%
  rename(time_pdt = time)

# Binarize sentiment (0 = negative, 1 = positive)
twitter_cleaned <- twitter_cleaned %>%
  mutate(sentiment = factor(sentiment, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Negative", "Positive")))

# Clean up the text
twitter_cleaned <- twitter_cleaned %>%
  mutate(text = str_to_lower(text),                          # lowercase
         text = str_remove_all(text, "@\\w+"),               # remove @mentions
         text = str_remove_all(text, "http\\S+|www\\S+"),    # remove URLs
         text = str_remove_all(text, "\\bi['’]ll\\b"),       # remove contractions
         text = str_remove_all(text, "\\bi['’]d\\b"),
         text = str_remove_all(text, "\\bi['’]m\\b"),
         text = str_remove_all(text, "\\bi['’]ve\\b"),
         text = str_remove_all(text, "[^a-z\\s]"),           # remove punctuation/numbers
         text = str_squish(text))                            # remove extra whitespace
# First create row_id entry for each tweet, select only row_id, sentiment vaue, and text
twitter_cleaned <- twitter_cleaned %>%
  mutate(row_id = row_number()) %>%
  select(row_id, sentiment, text)

Testing/Training Split

We split our data at this point to avoid data leakage from our TF-IDF, which allows us to get a more accurate estimate of our model performance.

# Testing Training Split
set.seed(1)

twitter_split <- initial_split(
  twitter_cleaned,
  prop = 0.80,
  strata = sentiment
)

twitter_train <- training(twitter_split)
twitter_test <- testing(twitter_split)

Tokenizing/TF-IDF

Training Data

# Unigrams TF-IDF
unigram_train <- twitter_train %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text) %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") %>%
  count(row_id, sentiment, word, name = "n") %>%
  bind_tf_idf(
    term = word,
    document = row_id,
    n = n
  )

head(unigram_train, n = 10)
## # A tibble: 10 × 7
##    row_id sentiment word          n    tf   idf tf_idf
##     <int> <fct>     <chr>     <int> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
##  1      1 Positive  hug           1 0.2    6.45  1.29 
##  2      1 Positive  indy          1 0.2    8.27  1.65 
##  3      1 Positive  indykitty     1 0.2   10.6   2.11 
##  4      1 Positive  sleep         1 0.2    4.08  0.816
##  5      1 Positive  tight         1 0.2    7.68  1.54 
##  6      2 Negative  bad           1 0.25   4.00  1.00 
##  7      2 Negative  dont          1 0.25   3.18  0.795
##  8      2 Negative  feel          1 0.25   4.01  1.00 
##  9      2 Negative  yeah          1 0.25   4.31  1.08 
## 10      3 Negative  celebs        1 0.143  9.48  1.35
top_unigram_words <- unigram_train %>%
  count(word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5000) %>%
  pull(word)

unigram_train <- unigram_train %>%
  filter(word %in% top_unigram_words)

unigram_train_wide <- unigram_train %>%
  select(row_id, sentiment, word, tf_idf) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = word,
    values_from = tf_idf,
    values_fill = 0,
    names_prefix = "word_"
  )
# Bigrams TF-IDF
bigram_train <- twitter_train %>%
  unnest_tokens(bigram, text, token = "ngrams", n=2)  %>%
  separate(bigram, c("word1", "word2"), sep = " ") %>%
  filter(!word1 %in% stop_words$word) %>%
  filter(!word2 %in% stop_words$word) %>%
  unite(bigram, word1, word2, sep = " ") %>%
  count(row_id, sentiment, bigram, name = "n") %>%
  bind_tf_idf(
    term = bigram,
    document = row_id,
    n = n
  )

head(bigram_train, n = 10)
## # A tibble: 10 × 7
##    row_id sentiment bigram              n    tf   idf tf_idf
##     <int> <fct>     <chr>           <int> <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
##  1      1 Positive  hug indykitty       1 0.25  10.3    2.56
##  2      1 Positive  indykitty sleep     1 0.25  10.3    2.56
##  3      1 Positive  sleep tight         1 0.25   8.64   2.16
##  4      1 Positive  tight indy          1 0.25  10.3    2.56
##  5      3 Negative  stalk celebs        1 1     10.3   10.3 
##  6      4 Negative  couldnt spend       1 0.333 10.3    3.42
##  7      4 Negative  family cuz          1 0.333 10.3    3.42
##  8      4 Negative  spend time          1 0.333  8.30   2.77
##  9      6 Positive  amazing jesus       1 1     10.3   10.3 
## 10      7 Negative  aa xd               1 0.143 10.3    1.46
top_bigram_words <- bigram_train %>%
  count(bigram, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5000) %>%
  pull(bigram)

bigram_train <- bigram_train %>%
  filter(bigram %in% top_bigram_words)

bigram_train_wide <- bigram_train %>%
  select(row_id, sentiment, bigram, tf_idf) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = bigram,
    values_from = tf_idf,
    values_fill = 0,
    names_prefix = "bigram_"
  )

Testing Data

We have to put the testing data in the same format. However, we don’t want the TF-IDF values for words that were only in the test set, because if we are treating it as ‘new data’ we wouldn’t have access to it.

# Unigram Testing Data
unigram_test <- twitter_test %>%
  select(row_id, sentiment, text) %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text) %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") %>%
  filter(word %in% top_unigram_words) %>%  # keep only words that were used in train tf-idf
  count(row_id, sentiment, word, name = "n") %>%
  bind_tf_idf(
    term = word,
    document = row_id,
    n = n
  )

unigram_test_wide <- unigram_test %>%
  select(row_id, sentiment, word, tf_idf) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = word,
    values_from = tf_idf,
    values_fill = 0,
    names_prefix = "word_"
  )

# to match number of cols, fill in 0's for words that were in training but not in testing
# after, both data frames should have 5002 columns (5000 words + sentiment + row_id)
missing_unigram_cols <- setdiff(
  names(unigram_train_wide),
  names(unigram_test_wide)
)

unigram_test_wide[missing_unigram_cols] <- 0

unigram_test_wide <- unigram_test_wide %>%
  select(all_of(names(unigram_train_wide)))
# Bigram Testing data
bigram_test <- twitter_test %>%
  select(row_id, sentiment, text) %>%
  unnest_tokens(bigram, text, token = "ngrams", n = 2) %>%
  separate(bigram, into = c("word1", "word2"), sep = " ") %>%
  drop_na(word1, word2) %>%
  filter(!word1 %in% stop_words$word) %>%
  filter(!word2 %in% stop_words$word) %>%
  unite(bigram, word1, word2, sep = " ") %>%
  filter(bigram %in% top_bigram_words) %>%   #do same as unigrams
  count(row_id, sentiment, bigram, name = "n") %>%
  bind_tf_idf(
    term = bigram,
    document = row_id,
    n = n
  )

bigram_test_wide <- bigram_test %>%
  select(row_id, sentiment, bigram, tf_idf) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = bigram,
    values_from = tf_idf,
    values_fill = 0,
    names_prefix = "bigram_"
  )

# Match column number again
missing_bigram_cols <- setdiff(
  names(bigram_train_wide),
  names(bigram_test_wide)
)

bigram_test_wide[missing_bigram_cols] <- 0

bigram_test_wide <- bigram_test_wide %>%
  select(all_of(names(bigram_train_wide)))

Creating Recipe

Set Up a 5 Folds Cross-Validation

#Unigram 5-fold CV
unigram_folds <- vfold_cv(unigram_train_wide, v = 5, strata = sentiment)

unigram_rec <- recipe(sentiment ~ ., data = unigram_train_wide) %>%
  # tells model to ignore "row_id" so it doesn't use it as a predictor
  update_role(row_id, new_role = "ID")
  #step_nzv(all_predictors()) # removes near-zero variance predictors to speed up computation and rule out unlikely predictors
#Bigram 5-fold CV
bigram_folds <- vfold_cv(bigram_train_wide, v = 5, strata = sentiment)

bigram_rec <- recipe(sentiment ~ ., data = bigram_train_wide) %>%
  update_role(row_id, new_role = "ID")

Creating the Model and Workflow

We will be using a Lasso Logistic Regression model

#Unigram Model
# define Lasso Logistic Regression model
lasso_spec <- logistic_reg(
  penalty = tune(), 
  mixture = 1) %>%
  set_engine("glmnet") %>%
  set_mode("classification")

unigram_lasso_wf <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(unigram_rec) %>%
  add_model(lasso_spec)
#Bigram Model
bigram_lasso_wf <- workflow() %>% 
  add_recipe(bigram_rec) %>% 
  add_model(lasso_spec)

Tuning and Gridding

Run the Model + Fit Workflow onto Training Data

First, we are going to test a lasso logistic regression model on unigram/bigram training data

#Unigram Model
lasso_grid <- grid_regular(penalty(), levels = 30)
lasso_tune <- tune_grid(unigram_lasso_wf,
  resamples = unigram_folds,
  grid = lasso_grid)

show_best(lasso_tune, metric = "roc_auc")
## # A tibble: 5 × 7
##    penalty .metric .estimator  mean     n  std_err .config         
##      <dbl> <chr>   <chr>      <dbl> <int>    <dbl> <chr>           
## 1 0.00386  roc_auc binary     0.795     5 0.000899 pre0_mod23_post0
## 2 0.00174  roc_auc binary     0.791     5 0.00174  pre0_mod22_post0
## 3 0.000788 roc_auc binary     0.778     5 0.00200  pre0_mod21_post0
## 4 0.000356 roc_auc binary     0.767     5 0.00200  pre0_mod20_post0
## 5 0.00853  roc_auc binary     0.762     5 0.000676 pre0_mod24_post0
#Bigram Model
lasso_grid <- grid_regular(penalty(), levels = 30)
bi_lasso_tune <- tune_grid(bigram_lasso_wf,
  resamples = bigram_folds,
  grid = lasso_grid)

show_best(bi_lasso_tune, metric = "roc_auc")
## # A tibble: 5 × 7
##    penalty .metric .estimator  mean     n std_err .config         
##      <dbl> <chr>   <chr>      <dbl> <int>   <dbl> <chr>

## 2 0.00174  roc_auc binary     0.677     5 0.00383 pre0_mod22_post0
## 3 0.000788 roc_auc binary     0.673     5 0.00356 pre0_mod21_post0
## 4 0.000356 roc_auc binary     0.671     5 0.00327 pre0_mod20_post0
## 5 0.000161 roc_auc binary     0.669     5 0.00305 pre0_mod19_post0

Now, we will try a Support Vector Machine (SVM) model

#Unigram SVM Model
uni_svm_rec <- recipe(sentiment ~ ., data = unigram_train_wide) %>%
  update_role(row_id, new_role = "ID")

svm_spec <- svm_linear(cost = tune()) %>%
  set_engine("LiblineaR") %>%
  set_mode("classification")

unigram_svm_wf <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(uni_svm_rec) %>%
  add_model(svm_spec)

svm_grid <- grid_regular(cost(), levels = 5)

svm_tune <- tune_grid(unigram_svm_wf,
  resamples = unigram_folds,
  grid = svm_grid,
  metrics = metric_set(accuracy))

show_best(svm_tune, metric = "accuracy")
## # A tibble: 5 × 7
##        cost .metric  .estimator  mean     n std_err .config        
##       <dbl> <chr>    <chr>      <dbl> <int>   <dbl> <chr>

## 2  2.38     accuracy binary     0.702     5 0.00295 pre0_mod4_post0
## 3 32        accuracy binary     0.702     5 0.00295 pre0_mod5_post0
## 4  0.000977 accuracy binary     0.702     5 0.00293 pre0_mod1_post0
## 5  0.0131   accuracy binary     0.702     5 0.00293 pre0_mod2_post0
bi_svm_rec <- recipe(sentiment ~ ., data = bigram_train_wide) %>%
  update_role(row_id, new_role = "ID")

bigram_svm_wf <- workflow() %>% 
  add_recipe(bi_svm_rec) %>% 
  add_model(svm_spec)

bi_svm_tune <- tune_grid(bigram_svm_wf,
  resamples = bigram_folds,
  grid = svm_grid,
  metrics = metric_set(accuracy))

show_best(bi_svm_tune, metric = "accuracy")

Bigram Network Graph

Note swine flu, jonas brothers, harry potter - dataset is from 2009

bigram_train_sep <- twitter_cleaned %>%
  unnest_tokens(bigram, text, token = "ngrams", n=2)  %>%
  separate(bigram, c("word1", "word2"), sep = " ") %>%
  drop_na(word1, word2) %>%
  filter(!word1 %in% stop_words$word) %>%
  filter(!word2 %in% stop_words$word) 

bigram_graph <- bigram_train_sep %>%
  count(word1, word2) %>%
  filter(n > 20) %>%
  graph_from_data_frame()

a <- grid::arrow(type = "closed", length = unit(.15, "inches"))

ggraph(bigram_graph, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(edge_alpha = n), show.legend = FALSE,
                 arrow = a, end_cap = circle(.07, 'inches')) +
  geom_node_point(color = "lightblue", size = 5) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name), vjust = 1, hjust = 1) +
  theme_void()

Sparsity of Test Matrices

This is useful for the results later - the first code chunk shows how sparse the test dataframe is, the second shows the median number of words that was matched to TF-IDF values from the training. This is important because the more words that are the same, the better our model is going to do.

Unigram Sparsity

unigram_predictors <- unigram_test_wide %>%
  select(-row_id, -sentiment)

mean(unigram_predictors == 0)
## [1] 0.9992031
unigram_test_wide %>%
  mutate(nonzero_unigrams = rowSums(across(-c(row_id, sentiment), ~ .x != 0))) %>%
  summarise(
    min_nonzero = min(nonzero_unigrams),
    mean_nonzero = mean(nonzero_unigrams),
    median_nonzero = median(nonzero_unigrams),
    max_nonzero = max(nonzero_unigrams)
  )
## # A tibble: 1 × 4
##   min_nonzero mean_nonzero median_nonzero max_nonzero
##         <dbl>        <dbl>          <dbl>       <dbl>
## 1           1         3.98              4          14

Bigram Sparsity

Note that for bigrams the median is lower so the model is likely going to do worse. This is partly because tweets are very short, so each tweet only has a few bigrams and since bigrams are more unique we are less likely to have seen it in the training data.

bigram_predictors <- bigram_test_wide %>%
  select(-row_id, -sentiment)

mean(bigram_predictors == 0)
## [1] 0.9997648
bigram_test_wide %>%
  mutate(nonzero_bigrams = rowSums(across(-c(row_id, sentiment), ~ .x != 0))) %>%
  summarise(
    min_nonzero = min(nonzero_bigrams),
    mean_nonzero = mean(nonzero_bigrams),
    median_nonzero = median(nonzero_bigrams),
    max_nonzero = max(nonzero_bigrams)
  )
## # A tibble: 1 × 4
##   min_nonzero mean_nonzero median_nonzero max_nonzero
##         <dbl>        <dbl>          <dbl>       <dbl>
## 1           1         1.18              1           5

Fitting the Best Model on the Test Set

Cross-validation identified the Lasso logistic regression as the strongest model for both the unigram and bigram feature sets. Here we take the best model from cross-validation, fit it on the full training data, and apply it to the test set. This gives an honest estimate of how each model performs on unseen tweets.

Unigram Model

# Pull the best penalty from cv (ranked by roc_auc)
best_unigram <- select_best(lasso_tune, metric = "roc_auc")

#Lock that penalty into the workflow
final_unigram_wf <- finalize_workflow(unigram_lasso_wf, best_unigram)

# Fit the finalized model on the FULL unigram training data
unigram_final_fit <- fit(final_unigram_wf, data = unigram_train_wide)

# Apply the fitted model ONCE to the  unigram test set.
unigram_test_pred <- unigram_test_wide %>%
  select(row_id, sentiment) %>%
  bind_cols(
    predict(unigram_final_fit, new_data = unigram_test_wide, type = "prob"),
    predict(unigram_final_fit, new_data = unigram_test_wide, type = "class")
  )

head(unigram_test_pred)
## # A tibble: 6 × 5
##   row_id sentiment .pred_Negative .pred_Positive .pred_class

## 2     19 Negative           0.347          0.653 Positive   
## 3     20 Negative           0.493          0.507 Positive   
## 4     21 Negative           0.842          0.158 Negative   
## 5     26 Positive           0.535          0.465 Negative   
## 6     27 Positive           0.158          0.842 Positive

Bigram Model

# Same procedure for the bigram feature set
best_bigram <- select_best(bi_lasso_tune, metric = "roc_auc")

final_bigram_wf <- finalize_workflow(bigram_lasso_wf, best_bigram)

bigram_final_fit <- fit(final_bigram_wf, data = bigram_train_wide)

bigram_test_pred <- bigram_test_wide %>%
  select(row_id, sentiment) %>%
  bind_cols(
    predict(bigram_final_fit, new_data = bigram_test_wide, type = "prob"),
    predict(bigram_final_fit, new_data = bigram_test_wide, type = "class")
  )
